R.q: Read the passage. Select the sentence that shows the passage is told from a third-person omniscient point of view.

parts.t: Nurse Kim Okafor checked the monitor and frowned at the patient's rising heart rate.
She wondered whether the new medication was to blame.
In the bed, Mr. Alvarez kept his eyes closed, secretly afraid that her frown meant bad news.
"I'll be right back," Kim said as she stepped into the hallway.
The hallway was quiet except for the hum of the ice machine.

sn.a: Nurse Kim Okafor checked the monitor and frowned at the patient's rising heart rate.
sn.b: She wondered whether the new medication was to blame.
sn.c: In the bed, Mr. Alvarez kept his eyes closed, secretly afraid that her frown meant bad news.
sn.d: "I'll be right back," Kim said as she stepped into the hallway.
sn.e: The hallway was quiet except for the hum of the ice machine.

R.w: An omniscient narrator can reveal the thoughts of more than one character. Sentence 2 gives Kim's thoughts, and sentence 3 also reveals Mr. Alvarez's private fear. Only an all-knowing narrator can report both.

n.a: This reports only an action and a facial expression, which any third-person narrator, including an objective one, could describe.
n.b: This reveals Kim's thoughts, but a third-person limited narrator can also report one character's thoughts, so it does not establish omniscience.
n.d: "I" appears inside quoted dialogue. Pronouns in a character's speech do not set the narrator's point of view.
n.e: A description of the setting fits any point of view and reveals no character's thoughts.

R.q:
Read the passage.

In 1928, Alexander Fleming returned from a vacation to find mold growing on one of his plates of bacteria, with a clear ring around it where the bacteria had died. He named the substance the mold produced penicillin, but he could not purify it in useful amounts. About a decade later, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford took up the problem, and in 1940 they showed that penicillin protected infected mice. The first human patients were treated in 1941. Mass production in the United States during World War II made the drug widely available by 1944, and the three scientists shared the Nobel Prize in 1945.

Which statement about the order of events is accurate?
o: The first human patients were treated before the mouse experiments.
Florey and Chain purified penicillin before Fleming gave it a name.
Mice were protected by penicillin a year before people were treated.
The Nobel Prize was awarded before mass production of the drug began.
R.w: The mouse experiments were in 1940 and the first human patients were treated in 1941, one year later.

n.0: Reverses the order: mice in 1940, people in 1941.
n.1: Reverses the order: Fleming named penicillin in 1928, about a decade before Florey and Chain began their work.
n.3: Reverses the order: wartime mass production made the drug widely available by 1944, and the prize came in 1945.

R.q:
The bus pulled up to the clinic at 8:02. A woman in a red coat stepped off first, holding a toddler on her hip. She walked to the front desk and set down a folder. "We have a nine o'clock with Dr. Lee," she said. The receptionist glanced at the clock, then at the folder. "You're early," she said. "Have a seat." The woman sat down by the window. The toddler pressed his hand against the glass and watched the bus pull away.

Which point of view does the author use?
o: third person limited
first person
third person omniscient
third person objective
R.w: The narrator reports only what could be seen and heard (arrivals, movements and dialogue) and never reveals any character's thoughts or feelings. That is third-person objective.

n.0: A limited narrator would reveal one character's thoughts, such as why the woman came early; none are given.
n.1: "We" and "you" appear only inside the dialogue. The narrator never speaks as "I."
n.2: An omniscient narrator would reveal several characters' thoughts; this narrator reveals none.

R.q:
Standing desks have become common in American offices. A 2019 study of 300 office workers found that those who used standing desks for six months reported less lower-back pain than those who did not. Standing desks cost between $250 and $700 at major office suppliers. Several workers in the study said they felt more alert in the afternoon. It is a well-established fact that a standing desk is the healthiest choice for any office.

Which of the following statements is an opinion, even though the author presents it as established?
o: Standing desks cost between $250 and $700 at major office suppliers.
Workers who used standing desks for six months reported less lower-back pain.
Several workers in the study said they felt more alert in the afternoon.
A standing desk is the healthiest choice for any office.
R.w: Calling something "the healthiest choice for any office" is a sweeping judgment. Labeling it "a well-established fact" does not make it one; the study supports a narrower finding about back pain, not a ranking of every option for every office.

n.0: Prices can be verified at the suppliers, so this is a fact.
n.1: This reports a study result that can be checked against the published study, so it is a fact.
n.2: "Felt more alert" describes a feeling, but the statement reports what workers said, which the study records can confirm. It is a fact about their reports.

R.q:
For a pharmacology class, Daniel is gathering sources on a common blood pressure medication. He has found four items in the college library's databases. His instructor asks students to label each source as primary, secondary, or tertiary and reminds them that the label depends on what a source does with information, not on where it is published or how technical it sounds.

Which of Daniel's sources is a secondary source?
o: A journal article reporting a clinical trial the authors ran on the drug
The de-identified records of patients who took part in a drug trial
A review article summarizing the findings of 40 studies on the drug
A pharmacology dictionary that defines the drug class in one entry
R.w: A review article analyzes and summarizes research that others conducted, which makes it a secondary source.

n.0: An article in which researchers report their own original trial is a primary source.
n.1: Patient records are raw data created during the study, so they are primary.
n.3: A dictionary compiles brief information from other sources, so it is tertiary.

R.q:
Critics have called the city's summer jobs program "a handout for kids who don't want to work." The numbers tell a different story. Last summer, 640 teenagers worked an average of 22 hours a week at parks, libraries and health clinics, and 91 percent of them completed the full eight weeks. Anyone who still sneers at these hardworking young people simply hasn't bothered to look at the facts.

Which phrase from the passage reveals the author's own bias?
o: worked an average of 22 hours a week at parks
91 percent of them completed the full eight weeks
a handout for kids who don't want to work
still sneers at these hardworking young people
R.w: "Sneers" casts the program's critics in a scornful light, and "hardworking young people" praises the teens with loaded, favorable wording. These are the author's own words, and they show a one-sided slant in favor of the program.

n.0: This is a checkable figure about hours worked, stated in neutral terms.
n.1: This is a checkable statistic about completion, stated in neutral terms.
n.2: These loaded words belong to the critics, whom the author quotes in order to argue against them. A view the author reports and refutes is not the author's own bias.

R.q:
Hurricane Delia tore across Port Ellis last weekend with winds of 120 miles per hour. It ripped the roofs from more than half of the town's homes, flooded the only bridge to the mainland and left 9,000 residents without power. At a press conference on Monday, Mayor Teresa Ruiz looked at the crowd of reporters and said, "We've had a bit of a rough week."

The mayor's statement is an example of which of the following?
o: understatement
allusion
hyperbole
personification
R.w: Calling a devastating hurricane "a bit of a rough week" makes the situation sound far less serious than it is. Deliberately downplaying something is understatement.

n.1: An allusion refers to a well-known person, place, event or work; the mayor refers to none.
n.2: Hyperbole is the opposite: exaggerating to make something seem bigger. The mayor makes the disaster sound smaller.
n.3: Personification gives human traits to a non-human thing; the mayor describes the town's week without giving any object human qualities.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Older adults who volunteer regularly tend to report better health than those who do not. In several long-term studies, retirees who volunteered a few hours a week were less likely to develop high blood pressure and more likely to stay physically active. Researchers think the benefits come partly from staying busy and partly from social contact, since loneliness is linked to poorer health in later life. Volunteering also gives many retirees a sense of purpose that paid work once provided. The studies cannot fully rule out that healthier people are simply more likely to volunteer in the first place. Even with that caution, the pattern has encouraged some senior centers to connect members with local charities.

Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Loneliness in later life is linked to poorer health among retired adults.
Senior centers should require their members to volunteer with local charities.
Older adults who volunteer tend to be healthier, likely because of activity, contact and purpose.
Researchers cannot yet tell whether volunteering improves health or healthy people volunteer more.
R.w: Most of the passage describes the link between volunteering and better health in older adults and the likely reasons (staying busy, social contact, purpose). The caution about healthier people volunteering is one qualifying sentence, so the main idea keeps the emphasis on the health link.

n.0: Too narrow: the loneliness link is offered as one explanation for the benefits, not as the central point.
n.1: Distortion: senior centers connect members with charities; the passage never says they should require volunteering.
n.3: Reversed emphasis: the caution is a single qualifying sentence, and the author says the pattern holds "even with that caution."

R.q:
Read the passage.

Marcus had rehearsed his speech for the scholarship committee a dozen times in front of the bathroom mirror. When he walked into the room, though, the five faces at the long table made his notes feel like someone else's words. He stumbled through the first paragraph, then stopped. For a long moment he said nothing. Then he folded the paper and told them about the winter his grandmother was sick, when he had learned to check her blood sugar and cook her meals before school, and how that winter had made him want to become a nurse. When he finished, one committee member was writing quickly, and another nodded. Outside, Marcus realized he could not remember a single line of the speech he had practiced.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: One winter Marcus cared for his sick grandmother before school, which made him want to become a nurse.
Nervous, Marcus abandoned his rehearsed speech and spoke from experience, which seemed to engage the panel.
Marcus won a nursing scholarship after he told the committee a moving story about his grandmother.
Marcus practiced a scholarship speech many times but forgot most of it when he faced the committee.
R.w: The passage moves from Marcus's preparation, to his loss of confidence, to his decision to speak from personal experience, to the committee's positive reaction. This option covers that whole arc without adding events.

n.0: This is the backstory Marcus tells, a detail inside the story rather than a summary of the passage.
n.2: Goes beyond the text: the committee seemed engaged, but the passage never says Marcus won the scholarship.
n.3: Covers only the first part of the story and leaves out what Marcus did instead and how the committee responded.

R.q: A hospital newsletter claims: "Since our hand-hygiene campaign began in March, compliance has risen every month on every unit." The table shows the percent of observed opportunities in which staff cleaned their hands. Select the cell that contradicts the newsletter's claim.
R.w: The claim requires every unit to rise from each month to the next. Pediatrics fell from 86% in April to 84% in May, so that cell contradicts the claim. Every other unit rises each month.

n.a1: ICU rose from 78% to 82%. It is lower than Pediatrics' 86% in April, but the claim compares each unit with its own previous month.
n.a3: ICU rose from 85% to 91%, the largest one-month gain, which supports the claim.
n.b1: 70% is the lowest value among these cells, but Med-Surg still rose from 64% in March.
n.b3: Med-Surg rose from 76% to 79%. A smaller gain is still a rise.
n.c3: Pediatrics rose from 84% to 88% in June. This is the recovery after the drop, not the drop itself.

R.q:
For a history project on nurses in World War I, Paige wants to explain how Lena Harlow, an American army nurse, felt about working near the front lines in France. Her teacher has asked students to present the nurse's own words and feelings rather than someone else's account of them. The school library has several items about Harlow and about nursing in the war.

Which source would best meet Paige's purpose?
o: A collection of the letters Harlow wrote home from France
A textbook chapter on the role of nurses in World War I
A biography of Harlow written in 1985 by her grand-niece
An encyclopedia entry that summarizes Harlow's nursing career
R.w: Letters Harlow wrote from France are a primary source in her own words, recorded at the time, which is exactly what the assignment asks for.

n.1: A textbook chapter describes nurses in general and is secondary.
n.2: Even a family member's biography is a secondary account that interprets Harlow's experience.
n.3: An encyclopedia entry is a tertiary summary, not Harlow's own words.

R.q:
The town of Brookfield added a Route 9 bus to its east side three years ago. The table shows average riders per weekday.
Year | Route 9 riders | All routes combined
Year 1 | 420 | 5,100
Year 2 | 610 | 5,350
Year 3 | 800 | 5,560
A town report says Route 9's growth came mostly from new apartment buildings along its path. Two more buildings on the route are scheduled to open next year, and no other changes to bus service are planned.

Which prediction is best supported by the passage and table?
o: Route 9 ridership will most likely keep rising next year as the new buildings open.
Route 9 will carry more riders next year than all of the other routes put together.
Ridership on all routes combined will climb to about 8,000 riders per weekday next year.
Riders from other routes will likely switch to Route 9, lowering ridership on those routes.
R.w: Route 9 grew by about 190 riders a year, the report ties that growth to new apartment buildings on the route, and two more buildings open next year. The cause is still in motion, so continued growth is the supported prediction.

n.1: The other routes carry about 4,760 riders; Route 9 would need to grow sixfold in one year to pass them.
n.2: Combined ridership grew by about 200 to 250 a year; a jump of about 2,400 over-extends the trend.
n.3: Ridership on the other routes rose slightly each year (4,680, 4,740, 4,760), so the trend does not show riders leaving them.

R.q:
Read the description of the bar graph.

Title: Emergency Department Visits at County Hospital, 2021 to 2025
Vertical axis: Visits per year (in thousands)
Horizontal axis: Year
Bar heights:
2021: 42
2022: 45
2023: 51
2024: 49
2025: 56
Source note: Each bar shows total visits for the calendar year, including patients who left before being seen. Source: County Hospital annual reports, published each March for the previous year.

According to the graph, between which two consecutive years did emergency department visits increase the most?
R.w: Find each year-to-year change: 2021 to 2022, +3; 2022 to 2023, +6; 2023 to 2024, -2; 2024 to 2025, +7. The largest increase, 7 thousand visits, is from 2024 to 2025.

n.0: Visits rose by 3 thousand, the smallest increase shown.
n.2: Visits rose by 6 thousand, a large jump but 1 thousand less than from 2024 to 2025.
n.3: Visits fell by 2 thousand, so this is a decrease.

R.q:
Read the passage.

In the Del Rio water district, the average resident uses about 92 gallons of water a day at home in summer and about 58 gallons a day in winter. The difference comes mostly from lawn watering, which makes up about 40 percent of summer use but only about 5 percent of winter use. Indoor use changes little across the year. Toilets account for the most indoor water, about 18 gallons per person per day, followed by showers at about 13 gallons and faucets at about 11. Replacing an older toilet with a high-efficiency model saves about 9 gallons per person per day.

According to the passage, which statement about winter water use in Del Rio is accurate?
o: Toilets use noticeably less water than they do in the summer months.
Lawn watering makes up about 40 percent of a resident's home use.
The average resident uses about 58 gallons of water a day at home.
Showers account for about 18 gallons per person per day indoors.
R.w: The first sentence gives winter home use as about 58 gallons a day for the average resident.

n.0: Contradicted: the passage says indoor use changes little across the year.
n.1: 40 percent is the summer share; lawn watering is about 5 percent of winter use.
n.3: 18 gallons is the figure for toilets; showers use about 13 gallons.

R.q:
In January, the cafeteria at Mercy Valley Hospital switched to a new coffee supplier. In February, the number of sick days taken by staff fell by 15 percent compared with January. The cafeteria manager announced that the new coffee is clearly better for staff health and asked the newsletter editor to feature it in the next issue. The manager did not mention that January had been the peak of the local flu season.

Which statement best describes the flaw in the manager's reasoning?
o: It rejects an opposing view by attacking the people who hold that view.
It draws a conclusion about every hospital from one hospital's records.
It assumes that its conclusion is true in order to prove that conclusion.
It assumes that because one event came first, it caused the second one.
R.w: Sick days fell after the coffee changed, so the manager concludes the coffee caused the drop. That is post hoc reasoning, and the end of flu season is a more likely explanation.

n.0: The manager does not respond to any opponent, so there is no personal attack.
n.1: The manager draws a conclusion about this hospital's staff, not about every hospital.
n.2: The manager offers a reason (fewer sick days) that is separate from the conclusion; the flaw is the causal leap.

R.q:
Our county's public pools close every year on Labor Day, even though September temperatures here average 88 degrees. According to the county parks report, pool attendance on the last two weekends of August averaged 1,400 swimmers a day. A splash pad, a ground-level area of water jets with no standing water, costs far less to staff than a pool. It is shameful that families with no air conditioning are left with nowhere to cool off. The county must keep at least one pool open through September. Call your commissioner today.

Which features of the passage indicate that its primary purpose is to persuade rather than to inform? Select all that apply.
o: the average September temperature
the instruction to call a commissioner today
the emotionally charged word "shameful"
the demand that the county keep a pool open
the attendance figures from the county parks report
the definition of a splash pad
R.w: Loaded language ("shameful"), a direct claim about what the county must do and a call to action are features that mark persuasive writing. They show the facts in the passage are being used to push readers toward an action.

n.0: A temperature figure is a neutral fact that could appear in any kind of text.
n.4: Statistics appear in informative and persuasive texts alike; the figures alone do not show the author's purpose.
n.5: Defining a term is a typical feature of informative writing, so the definition does not mark the passage as persuasive.

R.q:
Read the passage.

A survey of 300 first-year nursing students at one state university asked how many hours they slept on nights before exams. Most reported fewer than six hours, and about one in four reported fewer than four. Students who slept fewer than six hours were also more likely to report feeling anxious during the exam. The survey did not record exam scores. The university's counseling center has since added a workshop on planning study time, which it advertises during the first week of each semester.

Which statement goes beyond what the passage supports?
o: Short sleep before exams was linked to anxiety among students surveyed.
Students who slept fewer than six hours earned lower exam scores.
The counseling center now offers a workshop on planning study time.
Most of the students surveyed slept fewer than six hours before exams.
R.w: The passage says outright that the survey did not record exam scores, so no conclusion about scores can be drawn. The other three statements restate or directly follow from the passage.

n.0: Supported: students sleeping under six hours were more likely to report anxiety, which is a link, not a cause.
n.2: Supported: the passage says the counseling center added this workshop.
n.3: Supported: the passage says most students reported fewer than six hours.

R.q:
Read the passage.

At Juniper Elementary, the school garden began as four raised beds behind the gym. Third graders now plant lettuce, carrots and peas each spring, and the cafeteria serves the harvest at a salad bar one week each May. Teacher Rosa Lin, who started the garden, says that students who once refused anything green now ask for second helpings of the salad they grew. Last year, the parent group raised money to add eight more beds and a rain barrel. The principal has asked other teachers whether they would like to use the garden for science lessons.

Which statements are supported by the passage? Select all that apply.
o: The cafeteria serves vegetables from the garden throughout the spring.
Several other teachers now use the garden for their science lessons.
The garden has grown larger since it was first started.
The principal is interested in expanding how the garden is used.
The parent group paid for the original four raised beds.
According to Ms. Lin, some students eat more vegetables they grew.
R.w: The garden went from four beds to twelve. Ms. Lin reports students asking for seconds of the salad they grew. The principal asking other teachers about science lessons shows interest in wider use.

n.0: Distortion: the harvest is served at a salad bar one week each May, not throughout the spring.
n.1: Goes beyond the passage: the principal has asked teachers whether they would like to use it; nothing says any of them do yet.
n.4: Wrong detail: the parent group paid for the eight added beds and a rain barrel, not the original four.

R.q:
Read the directions.

Assembling the Shower Chair
Wait until the backrest is secure before you attach the four legs to the seat frame. Before you attach the backrest, slide the two rubber grips onto the armrests. The armrests themselves must be bolted to the seat frame before any other step, since the backrest screws pass through them. Once the legs are on, set the chair's height by pressing the push pins into matching holes on all four legs. Test the chair on a flat surface before use.

Place the assembly steps in the order the directions require, starting with the first.
o: Slide the rubber grips onto the armrests
Set the height with the push pins
Attach the backrest
Attach the four legs
Bolt the armrests to the seat frame
R.w: The armrests are bolted on before any other step because the backrest screws pass through them. The grips go on before the backrest. The legs wait until the backrest is secure, and the height is set once the legs are on.

R.q:
Read the memo.

MEMORANDUM
To: All Clinic Staff
From: Rafael Ortiz, Office Manager
Date: Monday, October 7
Re: Flu shot clinic for staff

Free flu shots for staff will be given in Conference Room B on Wednesday, October 16, from 7:00 to 9:00 a.m., and on Thursday, October 17, from 4:00 to 6:00 p.m. Sign up for a 10-minute slot on the sheet outside my office by Friday, October 11. Staff who received a flu shot elsewhere this season should email a copy of their record to Employee Health by October 31. Staff who cannot receive the vaccine for medical reasons must submit an exemption form, available from Employee Health, by the same date.

According to the memo, what is the deadline for signing up for a flu shot time slot?
o: Monday, October 7
Friday, October 11
Thursday, October 31
Wednesday, October 16
R.w: The memo says to sign up on the sheet outside the office manager's office by Friday, October 11.

n.0: October 7 is the date the memo was written.
n.2: October 31 is the deadline for outside vaccination records and exemption forms.
n.3: October 16 is the first day shots are given, not the sign-up deadline.

R.q:
To the Bellmont City Council:

Every school morning, about 300 students cross Route 6 to reach Lincoln Elementary. The road has no crosswalk within half a mile of the school, and cars there travel at an average of 41 miles per hour, according to the county's own traffic study. Last year, police recorded four collisions involving pedestrians on that stretch. A marked crosswalk with flashing lights would cost about $60,000, less than the city spent repaving the parking lot at City Hall. I urge you to fund it at your next meeting.

What is the author's primary purpose in this letter?
o: to describe the morning walk that students take to school
to persuade the council to install a crosswalk near the school
to inform readers about the county's traffic study on Route 6
to criticize the council for repaving the City Hall parking lot
R.w: The letter closes with a direct request ("I urge you to fund it"), and each fact is chosen to support that request. Facts that serve a claim make the purpose persuasive, not informative.

n.0: The students' crossing is mentioned to show the danger, not described in detail.
n.2: The traffic study is used as evidence for the request; the letter does not explain the study for its own sake.
n.3: The parking lot comparison is a single supporting point used to show the crosswalk is affordable; it is not the main aim of the letter.

R.q:
Passage 1
From a second-grade teacher: Studies of young children find little link between nightly homework and better grades. Worksheets often lead to tears at the kitchen table. I now ask families for one thing: read together for twenty minutes each night.

Passage 2
From a parent: My daughter's weekly homework packet does more than review math facts. It teaches her to manage her time and finish a task without being told twice. It also shows me what she is learning, so I can help when she struggles. I hope the school keeps assigning it.

The authors disagree most about whether
o: homework improves the grades of older students
reading at home each night benefits young children
young children should be given regular homework
parents should know what children learn at school
R.w: The teacher has replaced homework with shared reading because of weak evidence, while the parent wants the school to keep the weekly packet. Their conflict is over assigning homework to young children.

n.0: Both passages concern young children; neither discusses older students.
n.1: The teacher recommends nightly reading, and the parent never questions it, so this is not a point of disagreement.
n.3: The parent values knowing what her child learns; the teacher does not argue against it.

R.q:
For three years, Priya and Elena had finished first and second at the county science fair, always in that order. This spring, Priya's solar oven cracked the night before judging. At ten o'clock, Elena knocked on her door with a roll of foil, a glue gun, and her own notes on insulation. They worked until midnight. The next day Elena took first place, and Priya took third. Walking out of the gym, Priya expected to feel crushed. Instead, she found herself planning next year's project with Elena, and the ribbon in her pocket felt lighter than she had expected.

Which statement best expresses the theme of the passage?
o: Kindness from a rival can turn a competition into a friendship.
The long rivalry between two students at a county science fair
Elena helps Priya repair her solar oven on the night before the science fair.
Hard work is the surest path to winning first place in a contest.
R.w: A theme is a message about life stated as a complete idea. Elena's help changes Priya's feelings about losing and leads to shared plans, so the story's message is that a rival's kindness can build friendship.

n.1: This names the topic of the story in a phrase; it does not state a message about it.
n.2: This is a plot summary of one event, not the message the story conveys.
n.3: Priya worked hard yet placed third; the story's focus is the friendship, not a recipe for winning.

R.q:
Read the instructions.

Applying to the Nursing Program: Upload Instructions
Upload each document as a separate PDF no larger than 5 MB. Name each file with your last name, an underscore and the document type, for example Rivera_Statement.pdf. Transcripts must be official copies sent directly by your previous schools; do not upload transcripts yourself. Upload your TEAS score report, your immunization record and your personal statement. Your personal statement must be no longer than 500 words. Applications missing any required upload will not be reviewed.

Destiny Chen is preparing her files.

Which file follows the instructions?
o: Chen_Records.pdf, her immunization record and TEAS report together
Destiny_Statement.pdf, her 450-word personal statement
Chen_TEAS.pdf, a 2 MB copy of her TEAS score report
Chen_Transcript.pdf, a scan of her official college transcript
R.w: The TEAS score report is a required upload, the file is a single PDF under 5 MB, and the name follows the last name, underscore, document type pattern.

n.0: Each document must be uploaded as a separate PDF, not combined in one file.
n.1: The file name must begin with her last name (Chen), not her first name.
n.3: Transcripts must be sent directly by the schools; applicants are told not to upload them.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Each year, thousands of people in the United States wait for a kidney transplant, and many will wait more than three years.

Consider Ray Delgado, a 52-year-old bus driver from Tucson. Ray spends four hours at a dialysis center three mornings a week. He has given up his route, his weekend softball league and the road trips he once took with his grandchildren. "I'm alive," he says, "but I'm waiting to live."

A single living donor can end that wait. Most healthy adults can donate a kidney and lead normal lives afterward, and the donor's medical costs are generally covered. Anyone curious about donating can contact a transplant center for a free screening.

What is the most likely purpose of the second paragraph?
o: To give a personal example that makes the long wait feel real to readers
To present an opposing view on whether to become a living donor
To suggest that bus drivers face a higher risk of kidney disease
To explain the medical steps involved in kidney dialysis treatment
R.w: The first paragraph states a statistic about long waits. The second turns that number into one person's life: the hours on dialysis, the activities he gave up and his own words. The detail humanizes the problem before the final paragraph asks readers to consider donating.

n.1: Ray's story supports the case for donation; no opposing view appears in the passage.
n.2: Ray's job is a personal detail; the passage makes no claim about bus drivers' risk.
n.3: The paragraph mentions how long Ray spends at dialysis but never explains the treatment's steps.

R.q:
Passage 1
When Nadia's best friend Jo copied her homework, Nadia told the teacher she had shared her answers by accident. The teacher believed her. Jo kept copying, and by spring both girls were called in for a meeting with the principal. Afterward, Jo admitted she wished Nadia had just told her no.

Passage 2
Theo asked Sam what he thought of the song he had written. "Honestly? The chorus is boring," Sam said, and laughed. Theo did not touch his guitar for a week. Later, Sam tried again. He told Theo which lines he loved and suggested a faster beat for the chorus. Theo rewrote it that night.

How do the themes of the two passages differ?
o: Both passages suggest that friends should avoid difficult conversations to protect their friendships.
Passage 1 suggests lying to protect a friend is kind; Passage 2 suggests blunt honesty helps a friend most.
Passage 1 is about cheating at school, while Passage 2 is about writing music with a close friend.
Passage 1 shows the harm in covering for a friend; Passage 2 shows honest feedback works best given with care.
R.w: Nadia's cover story leads both girls into trouble, and Jo wishes Nadia had refused, so Passage 1 warns against covering for a friend. Sam's blunt comment hurts while his careful feedback helps, so Passage 2 is about delivering truth with care.

n.0: Both passages show that avoiding the truth or delivering it carelessly causes harm; neither recommends avoiding hard conversations.
n.1: Passage 1 shows the lie backfiring, and Passage 2 shows blunt honesty hurting Theo, so both halves misread the texts.
n.2: This contrasts the settings, not the messages the stories convey.

R.q:
The Okafor family is planning a day hike in the mountains tomorrow and wants to know whether thunderstorms are expected on the trail in the afternoon. They have found a National Weather Service seasonal outlook calling for a wetter-than-normal summer, the National Weather Service forecast for the hiking area that was updated this morning, this morning's forecast for their home city two hours' drive away, and a park ranger's post from yesterday about muddy conditions on the trail.

Which source should the family use?
o: The park ranger's post from yesterday about muddy conditions on the trail
This morning's forecast for their home city, two hours' drive from the trail
The National Weather Service forecast for the hiking area, updated this morning
The National Weather Service seasonal outlook calling for a wetter summer
R.w: The hiking-area forecast meets every need: it is current (updated this morning), covers the exact place and day, and comes from the national weather authority.

n.0: The ranger's post concerns the trail but describes yesterday's ground conditions, not a forecast of tomorrow's storms.
n.1: This forecast is current but covers a city two hours away; it does not describe afternoon storms in the mountains where they will hike.
n.3: The outlook comes from the right agency, but it covers the whole season, not tomorrow afternoon in the hiking area.

R.q:
Letter to the editor: Nearly everyone I know in Maple Heights has already signed the petition against the new cell tower on Birch Road, so the council should listen to the community and reject it. Think about your children sleeping a few hundred feet from that tower every single night. Do you really want to gamble with their health? Vote no before it is too late.

Which fallacies does the letter contain? Select all that apply.
o: Ad hominem
Straw man
Bandwagon
Appeal to false authority
Circular reasoning
Appeal to fear
R.w: "Nearly everyone I know has signed" argues from popularity (bandwagon). The image of children sleeping near the tower and "gamble with their health" try to frighten readers without any evidence of harm (appeal to fear).

n.0: The letter does not attack any person who supports the tower.
n.1: The letter never states or distorts an opponent's position.
n.3: No expert or celebrity is cited.
n.4: The letter's reasons (the petition, fear for children) are separate from its conclusion, even though they are weak.

R.q:
Supporters of the proposed ban on plastic grocery bags claim it will cut litter in our parks in half. The evidence from cities that have tried such bans suggests a smaller effect: studies in three comparable cities found that plastic bag litter fell, but overall park litter dropped by about 20 percent. Even so, I will vote for the ban. A 20 percent drop is real progress, the cost to shoppers is a reusable bag, and our parks crew spends hundreds of hours a year picking up plastic.

Which statement best expresses the author's own position?
o: The ban is worth adopting even if its effect is smaller than claimed.
The ban will cut park litter in half, as its supporters have claimed.
The ban should be rejected because its effect on park litter is modest.
The city should study the ban for another year before it votes on it.
R.w: The author doubts the supporters' 50 percent claim, citing a drop of about 20 percent, but says "Even so, I will vote for the ban" because that drop is real progress.

n.1: This is the supporters' claim, which the author reports and then questions.
n.2: The author calls the effect modest but supports the ban anyway.
n.3: The author does not call for more study and states a plan to vote for the ban.

R.q:
From a district newsletter: Students who used the MathBoost tutoring app for at least 30 minutes a week raised their end-of-semester test scores by an average of 12 points. Students who did not use the app raised their scores by an average of 4 points. MathBoost clearly helps students learn math, and the district should buy licenses for every middle school next year.

Which of the following, if true, would most seriously challenge the claim that the app helps students learn math?
o: Some students in the study used the app for more than two hours each week.
MathBoost would cost the district about $12 per student for each school year.
Most app users were in honors classes that covered more of the tested material.
Students who used the app said they enjoyed its game-style practice lessons.
R.w: Step 1: the claim is that the app caused the larger score gains. Step 2: if most app users were in honors classes that covered more tested material, the class, not the app, could explain the gap.

n.0: Heavy use by some students does not offer another explanation for the score difference.
n.1: Cost bears on whether to buy the app, not on whether it helps students learn.
n.3: Enjoyment is not evidence for or against learning gains.

R.q:
Last month, Lakeside Medical Center raised its parking fee for visitors to $28 a day. Families sitting at the bedsides of seriously ill loved ones, many of whom visit every day for weeks, now pay more than $800 a month simply to be present. The hospital made the change without a single public notice. This is an outrage, and the board owes these families an explanation and a refund.

Which word best describes the author's tone toward the hospital's decision?
o: resigned
indignant
sympathetic
sarcastic
R.w: "An outrage" and the demand for an explanation and a refund express anger at something the author considers unjust. Angry protest at an unfair act is an indignant tone.

n.0: "Resigned" means accepting something unwelcome as unavoidable, but the author demands that the board act.
n.2: The author does show sympathy, but toward the families. The question asks about the tone toward the hospital's decision, which is angry, not sympathetic.
n.3: Sarcasm says the opposite of what is meant; the author states the complaint directly.

R.q:
Read the paragraph.

(1) Have you ever noticed that a scrape on your face seems to heal faster than one on your shin? (2) The speed at which a wound heals depends largely on its blood supply. (3) Blood delivers the oxygen and nutrients that new tissue needs in order to grow. (4) The face and scalp have an especially rich network of small vessels, so wounds there often close within days. (5) The lower legs, farther from the heart, tend to heal more slowly. (6) Conditions that narrow blood vessels, such as smoking, can slow healing anywhere on the body.

Which sentence is the topic sentence of the paragraph?
o: Sentence 6
Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
R.w: Sentence 2 states the paragraph's central claim (healing speed depends on blood supply). Sentences 3 to 6 explain why and give examples: what blood delivers, fast healing in the face, slow healing in the legs, and narrowed vessels.

n.0: Sentence 6 is a final example of the same idea; a last sentence is not automatically the topic sentence.
n.1: Sentence 1 is a hook question that draws the reader in; it raises the topic but makes no claim.
n.3: Sentence 3 explains why blood supply matters, so it supports the topic sentence rather than stating it.

R.q:
Why should healthy adults get a flu shot every fall? Above all, the vaccine lowers your risk of serious illness, hospitalization and death from influenza. It also protects the people around you, including infants and older adults, who are more likely to become seriously ill. In addition, a flu shot can reduce the number of workdays and school days you miss. Finally, and least important for most people, vaccination can spare you a week of feeling miserable on the couch.

How does the author organize the reasons in the passage?
o: in chronological order, from the first event to the last
from the most important reason to the least important
by classifying adults into groups at different risk
by comparing vaccinated and unvaccinated adults
R.w: "Above all" introduces the strongest reason, and "least important for most people" marks the weakest at the end. Ranking reasons from most to least important is order-of-importance structure.

n.0: "Finally" can signal time order, but here it introduces the last reason in a ranked list, not the last event in a sequence.
n.2: Infants and older adults are mentioned as people who benefit, but the passage does not sort adults into risk categories.
n.3: The passage lists benefits of vaccination; it never describes unvaccinated adults for comparison.

R.q:
Read the description of the bar graph.

Title: Prescriptions Filled at Main Street Pharmacy, January to April
Vertical axis: Prescriptions (in hundreds)
Horizontal axis: Month
Bar heights:
January: 32
February: 28
March: 35
April: 30
Note: The pharmacy was closed for two days in February for remodeling. Source: pharmacy records. Each bar counts new prescriptions and refills together. The pharmacy hired a third technician in March to handle the extra work.

According to the graph, how many more prescriptions were filled in March than in February?
R.w: The axis is in hundreds. March (35 hundred = 3,500) minus February (28 hundred = 2,800) is 700 prescriptions.

n.1: Treats the axis as tens instead of hundreds.
n.2: Treats the axis as thousands instead of hundreds.
n.3: Subtracts the bar heights without applying the axis unit of hundreds.

R.q: Read the passage. Select the word that most clearly reveals the author's critical attitude toward the parking plan.

parts.t: announced

parts: a new parking plan. Visitors will now pay a $12 daily

parts.t: fee

parts: in the main garage, while staff must park in a

parts.t: remote

parts: lot and ride a shuttle. Hospital leaders call the change a

parts.t: necessary

parts: step to pay for garage repairs. For families who visit a sick relative every day, however, the plan

parts.t: gouges

parts: the people least able to absorb another bill.

R.w: "Gouges" means overcharges unfairly. Its strongly negative connotation is the author's own word choice, and it signals disapproval of the plan.

n.a: "Announced" is a neutral reporting verb with no positive or negative charge.
n.b: "Fee" is the plain, neutral term for a charge. The author could have chosen a loaded word here but did not.
n.c: "Remote" describes where the lot is. It states a location, not a judgment.
n.d: "Necessary" is a positive word, but it reports the hospital leaders' view, not the author's.

R.q:
As a firefighter for 22 years, I have been inside hundreds of homes after a fire, and I have learned which ones families walk out of. Our city should require landlords to install working smoke alarms in every bedroom of every rental unit. Smoke alarms give sleeping families the minutes they need to escape. The cost to a landlord is about $25 per alarm. Tenants should not have to buy their own safety.

In the first sentence, the author mainly uses which type of appeal?
o: Counterclaim, by stating a view the author rejects
Pathos, by describing a frightening fire in detail
Logos, by citing statistics on deaths in rental fires
Ethos, by establishing experience with the topic
R.w: The first sentence tells readers the author has 22 years of firefighting experience inside hundreds of homes. That builds credibility, an appeal to ethos.

n.0: The sentence presents no opposing view; it supports the author's authority.
n.1: The sentence describes the author's experience, not a vivid scene of a particular fire.
n.2: The first sentence gives no statistics; the only figure in the passage is the alarm cost, later.

R.q:
Last school year, three children were struck by cars while walking to Garfield Elementary. All three accidents happened at the Elm Street and Fourth Avenue intersections, the only crossings near the school without an adult crossing guard. The school board should hire two more crossing guards before classes start in August. The cost, about $18,000 a year, is small compared with the medical bills from even one serious injury.

Which assumption links the author's evidence to the claim?
o: Crossing guards lower the chance that children are struck at intersections.
The number of children walking to Garfield will rise in the coming school year.
Garfield's guarded crossings carry less car traffic than Elm Street and Fourth Avenue.
Drivers near Garfield are less careful than drivers in other parts of town.
R.w: The evidence is that accidents happened at crossings without guards; the claim is that guards should be hired. The argument works only if guards actually make those crossings safer for children.

n.1: The argument rests on last year's accidents at unguarded crossings; it does not depend on more children walking.
n.2: Lighter traffic at the guarded crossings would be another explanation for where the accidents happened, so it would weaken the argument rather than link it.
n.3: The argument compares crossings with and without guards, not drivers in different parts of town.

R.q:
Passage 1
From a public health official: Sugary drinks are the largest single source of added sugar in American diets. When the price of a product rises, people buy less of it. A tax of two cents per ounce would lower consumption and fund school nutrition programs.

Passage 2
From a community organizer: A soda tax takes the biggest bite from families who are already stretched thin, since they spend a larger share of their income on groceries. If we want people to drink fewer sugary drinks, we should fund clean water stations in parks and nutrition classes in schools.

Which assumption do the two authors share?
o: Low-income families buy more sugary drinks than other families.
A tax is the most effective way to cut sugary drink consumption.
Lowering sugary drink consumption would benefit public health.
Nutrition classes in schools have had little effect on habits.
R.w: The official proposes a tax to lower consumption, and the organizer says "if we want people to drink fewer sugary drinks" and offers other methods. Both take for granted that less consumption is desirable.

n.0: The organizer says lower-income families spend a larger share of income on groceries, not that they buy more soda.
n.1: This is the official's position; the organizer rejects the tax in favor of other approaches.
n.3: The organizer recommends nutrition classes, and the official does not discuss them.

R.q:
Jamal starts a new job at a medical office next Monday and plans to ride the Route 4 bus. At the start of this month, the city changed the times and stops on several bus routes. He has found four sources: a printed system map his roommate picked up last year, the transit authority's website, a blog where a regular rider reviews city bus routes, and a ride-share app that estimates travel times.

Which source will most reliably give Jamal the Route 4 departure times for next Monday?
o: The printed system map from last year, which lists every bus route
The rider's blog, which describes the usual delays on each route
The transit authority's website, which posts the current schedules
The ride-share app, which estimates door-to-door travel times
R.w: The transit authority runs the buses and posts the current schedule, which reflects this month's changes. It is both the most authoritative and the most current source.

n.0: Last year's map predates this month's changes, so its times may be wrong.
n.1: A rider's blog is unofficial and may not reflect the new schedule.
n.3: A ride-share app estimates car travel, not bus departure times.

R.q:
Read the passage.

At exactly 10:00 a.m., the fire alarm sounded on the fourth floor of Lincoln Hospital. At that same moment, the automatic fire doors swung shut, and every elevator returned to the ground floor and stopped. Nurses on the unit then closed the doors to patient rooms, beginning with the rooms closest to the stairwell. Two minutes later, the charge nurse called the operator to report that the unit was secure. The all-clear sounded at 10:12, after which the elevators were returned to service and the fire doors were reopened.

According to the passage, which event happened immediately after the elevators returned to the ground floor?
o: Nurses closed the doors to patient rooms.
The charge nurse called the hospital operator.
The automatic fire doors on the unit swung shut.
The all-clear sounded at 10:12.
R.w: The alarm, the fire doors and the elevators all acted "at that same moment." The next event, signaled by "then," is the nurses closing patient room doors.

n.1: The call to the operator came two minutes after the nurses closed the room doors.
n.2: The fire doors closed at the same moment as the elevators returned, not after.
n.3: The all-clear came at 10:12, several events later.

R.q:
Read the passage.

At a town meeting on the proposed walking trail, three speakers addressed the council. Parks director Helen Moore said the trail would cost about $1.2 million, mostly paid for by a state grant, and could open within two years. Dr. Kevin Asante, a family physician, argued that the trail would give residents a safe place to exercise and noted that many of his patients live more than a mile from any park. Business owner Lydia Chen supported the trail but asked the council to add parking near the downtown end, saying that trail users would otherwise fill the spaces her customers need. The council agreed to vote on the plan next month.

Which statement accurately reports what a speaker said?
o: Ms. Chen opposed the trail because it would take parking from her customers.
Ms. Moore said that the trail would be paid for mostly by local property taxes.
Dr. Asante said that many of his patients live more than a mile from a park.
Dr. Asante asked the council to add parking near the downtown end of the trail.
R.w: The passage reports that Dr. Asante noted that many of his patients live more than a mile from any park.

n.0: Ms. Chen supported the trail; she asked for added parking rather than opposing the plan.
n.1: Ms. Moore said the trail would be paid for mostly by a state grant, not local taxes.
n.3: Wrong speaker: the parking request came from Ms. Chen, not Dr. Asante.

R.q:
From a city magazine article: "Since the city launched its bike-share program in 2022, bike commuting has more than doubled."

U.S. Census survey: share of city workers who commute by bike
2021 | 1.8%
2022 | 2.1%
2023 | 2.6%
2024 | 3.0%

The census figures are estimates for the same city, based on a yearly survey of households; the 2021 figure was collected before the program existed.

Which statement best describes how the census data relate to the article's claim?
o: The data show a rise in bike commuting since 2022, but less than a doubling.
The data confirm that bike commuting more than doubled after the 2022 launch.
The data cannot be compared with the claim because they cover another city.
The data show that bike commuting declined after the program was launched.
R.w: From 2022 to 2024 the share rose from 2.1 to 3.0 percent, an increase of about 43 percent. That is real growth but well short of doubling (which would be 4.2 percent).

n.1: Doubling 2.1 percent would require 4.2 percent; the data reach 3.0.
n.2: The passage states that the census figures are for the same city.
n.3: The share rose every year after 2022, so the data show growth, not decline.

R.q:
Read the table.

Flu Vaccination Rates by Age Group, Pinewood Clinic Patients
Age group | 2023 | 2024 | 2025
18 to 34 | 31% | 34% | 38%
35 to 49 | 40% | 39% | 43%
50 to 64 | 52% | 55% | 54%
65 and older | 68% | 70% | 74%
Rates show the percentage of clinic patients in each age group who received a flu vaccine during the season.

Which statements are supported by the table? Select all that apply.
o: The 50-to-64 group's rate fell slightly from 2024 to 2025.
The 65-and-older group had the highest rate in every year shown.
The 35-to-49 group's rate rose each year from 2023 to 2025.
The 18-to-34 group's rate will pass 50 percent by the year 2028.
The 18-to-34 group's rate rose each year from 2023 to 2025.
More patients age 65 and older were vaccinated than patients 18 to 34.
R.w: The 65-and-older row is highest in each column (68%, 70%, 74%). The 18-to-34 row rises 31%, 34%, 38%. The 50-to-64 row drops from 55% to 54% between 2024 and 2025.

n.2: The 35-to-49 rate dipped from 40% to 39% in 2024 before rising.
n.3: Extrapolates beyond the table, which shows data only through 2025.
n.5: The table gives percentages within each group, not numbers of patients, so counts cannot be compared.

R.q:
The Main Street Farmers Market has operated every summer since 2018. Supporters say it has transformed downtown. In its best season, 2022, the market drew 48,000 visitors, and nearby shops reported their strongest summer sales in a decade. Vendors praise the friendly crowds and the shaded location along the river. Clearly, the market is a success that deserves a permanent city subsidy of $75,000 a year.

Which feature of the passage most strongly suggests a biased presentation?
o: It reports figures from the market's best year and omits the others.
It includes specific numbers about visitors and the size of the subsidy.
It states the author's conclusion in the final sentence of the passage.
It describes vendors' opinions about the crowds and the location.
R.w: The market has run for several seasons, yet the author reports figures from only its best one. Choosing the most favorable data while leaving out the rest (cherry-picking) gives a one-sided picture and signals bias.

n.1: Specific numbers can make a passage more balanced, not less. The problem is which numbers were chosen, not that numbers appear.
n.2: Placing a conclusion at the end is a structural choice that any writer, biased or not, might make.
n.3: Reporting what vendors say is a normal way to add detail; it does not by itself slant the presentation.

R.q:
Follow the directions.

Six chairs stand in a row, numbered 1 to 6 from left to right. Ana sits in chair 1, Ben in chair 2, Cruz in chair 3, Dev in chair 4, Eli in chair 5 and Fay in chair 6. Carry out the steps below in order.
1. Ana and Fay trade seats.
2. The person in chair 3 trades seats with the person in chair 5.
3. The person sitting immediately to the right of Ben trades seats with Ana.
4. Dev trades seats with whoever is in chair 1.

Who sits in chairs 1 through 6 after step 4?
o: Dev, Ben, Ana, Fay, Eli, Cruz
Fay, Ben, Dev, Ana, Cruz, Eli
Dev, Ben, Ana, Fay, Cruz, Eli
Dev, Ben, Eli, Ana, Cruz, Fay
R.w: Step 1: Fay, Ben, Cruz, Dev, Eli, Ana. Step 2 swaps chairs 3 and 5: Fay, Ben, Eli, Dev, Cruz, Ana. Step 3: Eli is right of Ben and trades with Ana: Fay, Ben, Ana, Dev, Cruz, Eli. Step 4: Dev trades with Fay in chair 1: Dev, Ben, Ana, Fay, Cruz, Eli.

n.0: Skips step 2, so Cruz and Eli never trade seats.
n.1: Has Dev trade with Ana, who started in chair 1, instead of whoever is in chair 1 after step 3.
n.3: Uses the person to the left of Ben (Fay) in step 3 instead of the person to the right.

M.q: A scuba diver is 42 feet below the surface (-42 ft). She swims to a depth of 17 feet below the surface (-17 ft). Which describes the change in her position?
o: 59 ft down
25 ft down
59 ft up
25 ft up
M.w: Change = final - initial = -17 - (-42) = -17 + 42 = 25. A positive change means she rose 25 feet.

n.0: 59 adds the depths, and the direction is also wrong; -17 is closer to the surface.
n.1: The change is positive (-17 is above -42), so she moved up, not down.
n.2: 59 adds the two depths (42 + 17) instead of finding the difference.

M.q: The bar graph shows the number of flu tests a clinic ran each month. Select the month whose value equals the mean number of tests for the six months.

n.c: March is one of the two bars in the middle of the graph, but position on the graph is not the center of the data. 25 is below the mean of 27, and the median is (25 + 27) / 2 = 26.
n.d: 18 is the minimum, well below the mean of 27.
n.e: 40 is the maximum, well above the mean of 27.

M.q: A scatterplot shows the hours of sleep the night before (x) and reaction time on a driving test, in milliseconds (y), for 25 adults. The points fall close to a straight line that slopes downward from left to right. Which best describes the relationship?
o: No correlation
Strong positive correlation
Weak negative correlation
Strong negative correlation
M.w: A downward slope from left to right means that as x increases, y tends to decrease: a negative correlation. Points close to a line make it strong.

n.0: No correlation is a cloud with no direction; these points follow a clear line.
n.1: A positive correlation rises from left to right; this pattern falls.
n.2: A weak correlation has widely scattered points; these fall close to the line.

M.q: An IV of 1,500 mL is ordered to infuse over 12 hours. After 5 hours, 700 mL have infused. At what rate must the rest of the IV run so that it finishes on time? Round to the nearest whole number.
o: 160 mL per hour
114 mL per hour
140 mL per hour
125 mL per hour
M.w: Volume left: 1,500 - 700 = 800 mL. Time left: 12 - 5 = 7 hours. Rate = 800 ÷ 7 = 114.29, which rounds to 114 mL per hour.

n.0: This divides the remaining 800 mL by the 5 hours already used instead of the 7 hours left.
n.2: This is the rate so far, 700 ÷ 5, not the rate needed for the remaining volume.
n.3: This is the original rate, 1,500 ÷ 12. The IV is ahead of schedule (700 mL infused instead of 625 mL), so 125 mL per hour for 7 more hours would deliver 1,575 mL and finish early.

M.q: During a quality check, 5 out of every 16 IV bags sampled had a label printed off-center. What percent of the sampled bags had an off-center label? Enter the number only, without the percent sign.

tr.3.125: Moved the decimal point only 1 place right.
tr.0.3125: Left the answer as a decimal instead of converting to a percent.

M.w: 5/16 = 5 ÷ 16 = 0.3125. Multiply by 100 to write it as a percent: 0.3125 × 100 = 31.25, so 31.25%.

M.q: A square floor tile in a hospital lobby has an area of 0.81 square meter. What is the length of one side of the tile?
M.w: Side = √0.81. Because 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81, the side is 0.9 m.

n.0: 0.405 is 0.81 ÷ 2; a square root is not half the number.
n.3: 0.2025 is 0.81 ÷ 4, which treats the area like a perimeter.

M.q: A cylindrical water tank behind a rural clinic has a radius of 3 feet and a height of 5 feet. What is the volume of the tank? Use 3.14 for pi.
o: 94.2 ft³
47.1 ft³

n.1: This uses the diameter (6 ft) as the radius.
n.2: This uses 2πrh, the area of the curved side, instead of πr²h.
n.3: This multiplies pi by the radius once (3.14 × 3 × 5) instead of by r².

M.q: The dose of a medicine varies directly with a patient's body weight. A patient who weighs 60 kg receives 150 mg. What dose, in milligrams, should a patient who weighs 84 kg receive?

tr.107.1: treating it as inverse variation (150 x 60 / 84)
tr.2.5: the constant of variation, not the dose

M.w: Direct variation: dose = k x weight. k = 150 / 60 = 2.5 mg per kg. Dose = 2.5 x 84 = 210 mg.

M.q: If a = -3 and b = 4, what is the value of the expression 2a² + 5b - ab? Enter your answer as a number.

tr.68: Squared 2a instead of squaring a alone.

M.q: The table shows quiz scores for nine students, grouped by study team. Select the score that is the median of all nine scores.
M.w: In order: 61, 76, 78, 83, 85, 88, 90, 92, 95. With nine values, the median is the 5th value, 85.

n.a1: 92 is the 8th of 9 values in order.
n.a2: 78 is the 3rd of 9 values in order.
n.a3: 88 is the 6th of 9 values in order, just above the median.
n.b1: 61 is the minimum, the 1st value in order.
n.b2: 83 sits in the center of the table and is the score closest to the mean (748 / 9, about 83.1), but in order it is the 4th of 9 values, not the 5th.
n.b3: 95 is the maximum, the 9th value in order.
n.c2: 76 is the 2nd of 9 values in order.
n.c3: 90 is the 7th of 9 values in order.

M.q: Four tables each use the x-values 1, 2, 3, 4. Which set of y-values shows a linear relationship between x and y?
M.w: A relationship is linear when equal steps in x give equal differences in y. Here y rises by 3 each time (5, 8, 11, 14).

n.0: The differences are 2, 4, 6, which are not constant.
n.1: These are the squares of x; the differences are 3, 5, 7.
n.3: Each y doubles (a constant ratio), which is exponential; the differences are 2, 4, 8.

M.q: A line graph shows an infant's weight at monthly checkups, with the vertical axis marked every 2 pounds. Birth: on the 8-pound line. 1 month: halfway between 10 and 12. 2 months: on the 12-pound line. 3 months: halfway between 12 and 14. 4 months: on the 14-pound line. What was the mean weight gain per month from birth to 4 months?
o: 6 pounds
1.5 pounds
3 pounds
1.2 pounds
M.w: Total gain = 14 - 8 = 6 pounds over 4 months (birth to month 4 is 4 intervals). Mean gain = 6 / 4 = 1.5 pounds per month.

n.0: 6 pounds is the total gain over 4 months, not the gain per month.
n.2: 3 pounds is the gain in the first month only (8 to 11, the point halfway between 10 and 12).
n.3: 6 / 5 = 1.2 divides by the 5 checkups instead of the 4 one-month intervals between them.

M.q: After a 20% discount, a home blood pressure monitor costs $52. What was the original price of the monitor?
M.w: The sale price is 80% of the original: 0.80 × original = 52. Original = 52 ÷ 0.80 = $65. Check: 20% of 65 is 13, and 65 - 13 = 52.

n.0: This adds 20 dollars instead of reversing a 20% discount.
n.2: This adds 20% of $52 to $52. The 20% was taken from the original price, so divide by 0.80 instead.
n.3: This takes another 20% off $52 instead of finding the price before the discount.

M.q: A clinic can buy exam gloves in a box of 100 for $8.40 or in a case of 10 such boxes for $76.50. How much is saved per glove by buying the case instead of single boxes?
o: 0.75 cent
0.075 cent
75 cents
7.5 cents
M.w: Single box: $8.40 ÷ 100 = $0.084 per glove. Case: $76.50 ÷ 1,000 = $0.0765 per glove. Savings: 0.084 - 0.0765 = $0.0075 per glove, which is 0.75 cent.

n.1: Decimal slip: $0.0075 is 0.75 cent; this moves the decimal one place too far.
n.2: This is the savings per box of 100 gloves ($8.40 - $7.65), not per glove.
n.3: Decimal slip: $0.0075 is 0.75 of a cent, not 7.5 cents.

M.q: A dietary aide converted six US customary measurements. Select the conversion that is incorrect.
M.w: 1 qt = 2 pt and 1 pt = 2 cups, so 1 qt = 4 cups and 3 qt = 3 x 4 = 12 cups. The listed 6 cups uses 1 qt = 2 cups.

n.d: 1 gal = 4 qt = 8 pt, so 1.5 x 8 = 12 pt.
n.f: 1 cup = 8 fl oz, so 48 / 8 = 6 cups. The same answer as the 3 qt row is correct here.

M.q: In a pie chart of a clinic's annual expenses, the medical supplies sector has a central angle of 54°. Medical supplies cost $13,500 for the year. What were the clinic's total annual expenses? Enter the number of dollars only, without commas.

tr.15: the supplies percent, not the total
tr.250: 13,500 / 54, treating the angle as the percent
tr.2025: 13,500 x 0.15, applying the percent instead of dividing by it

M.w: Fraction of the whole: 54 / 360 = 0.15 (15%). Supplies = 0.15 x total, so total = 13,500 / 0.15 = $90,000.

M.q:
A stem-and-leaf plot shows hemoglobin levels, in g/dL, for 11 blood donors (key: 12 | 4 = 12.4).
11 | 2 6 8
12 | 0 4 4 9
13 | 1 5 7
14 | 3
How many donors had a hemoglobin level below 12.5 g/dL?
M.w: Values below 12.5: 11.2, 11.6, 11.8, 12.0, 12.4, 12.4. Each leaf is one donor, so the repeated 4 counts twice: 6 donors.

n.0: 7 includes 12.9, which is above 12.5.
n.1: 5 counts the repeated leaf 12.4 once; each leaf is a separate donor.
n.3: 3 counts only the 11 stem and misses 12.0, 12.4 and 12.4.

M.q: A morning section of 12 students had a mean quiz score of 75, and an afternoon section of 28 students had a mean quiz score of 85. What is the mean quiz score of all 40 students?

n.0: (12 x 85 + 28 x 75) / 40 = 78 swaps the section sizes.
n.1: The larger section pulls the mean toward 85, but the 12 lower scores still count.
n.3: (75 + 85) / 2 = 80 averages the two means, ignoring that the sections have different sizes.

M.q: Brand A oatmeal costs $5.28 for a 1.5-pound canister. Brand B oatmeal costs $4.60 for a 20-ounce canister. Which brand costs less per ounce, and by how much per ounce?
o: Brand B, by $0.12 per ounce
Brand A, by $0.01 per ounce
Brand B, by $0.06 per ounce
Brand A, by $0.16 per ounce
M.w: 1.5 lb × 16 = 24 oz. Brand A: $5.28 ÷ 24 = $0.22 per oz. Brand B: $4.60 ÷ 20 = $0.23 per oz. Brand A is cheaper by $0.01 per ounce.

n.0: This treats 1.5 lb as 15 oz. Since 1.5 lb = 24 oz, Brand A costs $0.22 per ounce.
n.2: This uses 12 oz per pound (1.5 lb = 18 oz); 1 lb = 16 oz.
n.3: $0.16 is the difference per pound ($3.52 vs. $3.68), not per ounce.

M.q: A lawn sprinkler waters a circular region with an area of 113.04 square meters. A landscaper needs the width of the region measured straight across through its center. What is the diameter of the watered region? Use 3.14 for pi.
o: 6 m

n.0: 6 m is the radius; the diameter is twice the radius.
n.2: This divides the area by 2π (6.28), as if A = 2πr.
n.3: 36 is r²; take its square root to find r, then double it.

M.q: A number line has tick marks labeled -3 and 5, with 3 unlabeled tick marks evenly spaced between them. What value does the second unlabeled tick mark to the right of -3 represent?
M.w: 3 tick marks between the labels create 4 equal intervals. The distance from -3 to 5 is 8, so each interval is 8 ÷ 4 = 2. Second tick: -3 + 2 × 2 = 1.

n.0: -1/3 divides 8 into 3 intervals and stops at the first tick.
n.1: 2 1/3 divides 8 into 3 intervals; 3 tick marks between the labels make 4 intervals.
n.3: -1 is the first unlabeled tick (-3 + 2), not the second.

M.q: Jordan earns $2,850 per month after taxes. Each month he pays $1,140 in rent, spends 1/6 of his after-tax income on food and puts $300 into savings. How much money does he have left each month?

n.0: $1,235 leaves out the $300 put into savings.
n.1: $1,410 leaves out the food spending.
n.2: $1,125 takes 1/6 of the money left after rent ($285) instead of 1/6 of his income.

M.q: A printer in a clinic prints 18 pages in 45 seconds. At this rate, how many pages can it print in 4 minutes?
M.w: Convert first: 4 minutes = 240 seconds. Set up 18/45 = p/240. Cross-multiply: 45p = 4,320, so p = 96 pages.

n.0: This treats 18 pages as the number printed per minute, multiplying 18 by 4.
n.1: This divides 45 by 18 and multiplies by 4, which inverts the rate.
n.3: This mixes units, comparing 4 minutes with 45 seconds without converting 4 minutes to 240 seconds.

M.q: A disinfectant is mixed so that 3/40 of the final solution is concentrate and the rest is water. What percent of the final solution is concentrate? Enter the number only, without the percent sign.

tr.0.075: Left the answer as a decimal instead of a percent.
tr.0.75: Moved the decimal point only 1 place right.
tr.92.5: Found the percent that is water (100 - 7.5) instead of concentrate.

M.w: 3/40 = 3 ÷ 40 = 0.075. Multiply by 100: 0.075 × 100 = 7.5, so 7.5% of the solution is concentrate.

M.q: An IV bag holds 1,000 mL. It infuses at a constant rate of r mL per hour, and after 8 hours, 280 mL remain in the bag. The equation 1,000 - 8r = 280 models the situation. What is r?
o: 160 mL per hour
35 mL per hour
90 mL per hour
125 mL per hour
M.w: 1,000 - 8r = 280. Subtract 1,000 from both sides: -8r = -720. Divide by -8: r = 90 mL per hour. Check: 8 × 90 = 720 mL infused, and 1,000 - 720 = 280 mL left.

n.0: Sign error: this adds 280 to 1,000, giving 8r = 1,280. The 280 mL left must be subtracted from 1,000.
n.1: This divides the amount remaining by 8 hours. The rate comes from the amount infused, 720 mL.
n.3: This divides the full 1,000 mL by 8 hours, as if the bag had emptied.

M.q: Data set A is 14, 18, 22, 26, 30. Data set B is 8, 21, 22, 23, 36. Which statement correctly compares the two data sets?
o: Same mean and median, but B has the greater range
Same mean and range, but the medians differ
Same mean and median, but A has the greater range
Same median, but B has the greater mean and range
M.w: A: sum 110, mean 22, median 22, range 30 - 14 = 16. B: sum 110, mean 22, median 22, range 36 - 8 = 28. Same center, but B is more spread out.

n.1: Both medians are 22 (the 3rd value of 5), and the ranges are 16 and 28, not equal.
n.2: A's evenly spaced values span only 30 - 14 = 16, while B's span 36 - 8 = 28.
n.3: B's values also sum to 110, so both means are 22; only the ranges differ (16 and 28).

M.q: A uniform shop applies a sequence of price changes to a scrub set that starts at $50. Which sequences give a final price of $40.50? Select all that apply.
o: A 25% decrease followed by an 8% increase
A 15% decrease followed by a 4% decrease
A 10% decrease followed by a 9% decrease
A single 19% decrease
A 20% decrease followed by a 1% increase
A 10% decrease followed by another 10% decrease

n.1: 0.85 × 0.96 = 0.816, giving $40.80. Successive percents multiply; they do not add to 19%.
n.2: 0.90 × 0.91 = 0.819, giving $40.95. The 9% applies to $45, not to $50.
n.4: 0.80 × 1.01 = 0.808, giving $40.40. Adding the percents (-20% + 1% = -19%) does not work for successive changes.

M.q: A student is checking which expressions are equivalent to 3(2x - 4) + 2x. Select all that apply.
M.w: Simplify: 3(2x - 4) + 2x = 6x - 12 + 2x = 8x - 12. Check the factored forms: 4(2x - 3) = 8x - 12 and 2(4x - 6) = 8x - 12, so both are equivalent.

n.2: This equals 5(2x - 4), as if the 2x outside the parentheses were added to the 3. The 2x is a separate term, not part of the multiplier.
n.3: Sign error: 3 × (-4) = -12, not +12.
n.5: This distributes the 3 to 2x but not to -4. 3(2x - 4) = 6x - 12, so the constant is -12.

M.q: Solve for x: x/6 + 4 = 11.
M.w: Subtract 4 from both sides: x/6 = 7. Multiply both sides by 6: x = 42. Check: 42/6 + 4 = 7 + 4 = 11.

n.0: Sign error: 4 was added to 11 instead of subtracted, giving x/6 = 15.
n.1: This divides by 6 instead of multiplying. To undo x/6, multiply both sides by 6.
n.3: This multiplies 11 by 6 but not the 4. Multiplying every term by 6 gives x + 24 = 66, so x = 42.

M.q: Solve the proportion 6/x = 15/40.
M.w: Cross-multiply: 15x = 6 × 40 = 240. Divide by 15: x = 16. Check: 6/16 = 0.375 and 15/40 = 0.375.

n.0: This multiplies 15 by 40 and divides by 6, pairing the wrong terms when cross-multiplying.
n.2: This uses addition: 15 is 9 more than 6, so it takes 9 from 40. Proportions scale by multiplying, not adding.
n.3: This flips the second ratio, solving 6/x = 40/15, which gives 40x = 90.

M.q: A traveler rents a car in Canada, where gasoline costs $1.70 per liter. The car's tank holds 12 gallons. Use 1 gallon = 3.785 liters. How much will it cost to fill the empty tank? Enter the number of dollars, rounded to the nearest dollar.

tr.5: Divided 12 by 3.785 (3.17 L) instead of multiplying.
tr.20: Multiplied 12 by $1.70 without converting gallons to liters.

M.q: Five values are to be plotted on a number line: |-2.5|, -|3|, -2 1/4, 1.9 and |-1/2|. Place them in order from left to right on the number line, starting with the leftmost.
M.w: Evaluate each first: -|3| = -3, -2 1/4 = -2.25, |-1/2| = 0.5, 1.9, |-2.5| = 2.5. Left to right is least to greatest: -3 < -2.25 < 0.5 < 1.9 < 2.5. Note that |-2.5| is positive, while -|3| is negative because the negative sign is outside the bars.

M.q: A wooden deck is shaped like a trapezoid. Its parallel sides are 18 feet and 12 feet long, and the perpendicular distance between them is 8 feet. What is the area of the deck?
o: 120 ft²
144 ft²
240 ft²
96 ft²

n.1: This multiplies the longer base by the height, as if the deck were a rectangle.
n.2: This adds the bases and multiplies by the height but leaves out the 1/2.
n.3: This multiplies the shorter base by the height, as if the deck were a rectangle.

M.q: A rectangular patient room measures 14 feet by 11 feet. New vinyl flooring costs $4.25 per square foot, including installation. What is the total cost to cover the entire floor of the room?

n.1: This takes half of the area, as if the floor were a triangle.
n.2: This uses 14 + 11 = 25, half the perimeter, instead of the area.
n.3: This uses the perimeter (2 × 14 + 2 × 11 = 50 ft) instead of the area.

M.q: To estimate 6.8 × 4.6, a student rounds both numbers to the nearest whole number and calculates 7 × 5 = 35. How does this estimate compare with the exact product?
o: An exact estimate, because the rounding errors are both less than 0.5
An underestimate, because 4.6 was rounded more than 6.8
An overestimate by 0.6, the total amount the factors were rounded up
An overestimate, because both factors were rounded up
M.w: Both factors were rounded up (6.8 → 7 and 4.6 → 5), so the estimate is too high. Exact: 6.8 × 4.6 = 31.28, so 35 is 3.72 too high.

n.0: The rounding errors are small, but they still change the product (35 vs 31.28).
n.1: Rounding both factors up makes the product larger, so the estimate is too high, not too low.
n.2: The round-offs are multiplied by the other factors, so the error is 35 - 31.28 = 3.72, not 0.6.

M.q: A regional hospital system reported serving 248,513 patients last year. What is this number rounded to the nearest ten thousand?
M.w: The ten-thousands digit is 4 (in 248,513). The digit to its right is 8, which is 5 or more, so round up: 250,000.

n.0: 200,000 is rounded to the nearest hundred thousand.
n.1: 249,000 is rounded to the nearest thousand.
n.3: 240,000 truncates; the thousands digit 8 means rounding up.

M.q: The bar graph shows the number of patients admitted to a hospital unit each month. Select the month with the largest decrease from the month before.
M.w: Month-to-month changes: Feb -6, Mar +13, Apr -16, May +5, Jun -11, Jul +3. The largest decrease is April (71 to 55, a drop of 16).

n.a: January is the first month shown, so there is no earlier month to compare it with.
n.b: February fell by 6 (64 to 58), a smaller drop than April's 16.
n.c: March has the largest change in the other direction: it rose by 13 (58 to 71).
n.f: June has the lowest value (49), but it fell only 11 from May's 60.

M.q: A patient in a weight-management program weighed 182 pounds at week 2 and 173 pounds at week 6. What was the average rate of change in the patient's weight over this period?
o: -2.25 pounds per week
-0.44 pounds per week
-4.5 pounds per week
-1.5 pounds per week
M.w: Rate of change = change in weight ÷ change in time = (173 - 182) ÷ (6 - 2) = -9 ÷ 4 = -2.25 pounds per week.

n.1: This divides the weeks by the pounds (4 ÷ 9), which inverts the rate.
n.2: This divides the 9-pound change by 2, the starting week number, instead of the 4 weeks that passed.
n.3: This divides the 9-pound change by 6, the week number, instead of the 4 weeks that passed.

S.q: A student sorting metric rulers and measuring tools by scale is asked to rank five lengths. Place the lengths in order from largest to smallest, starting with the largest.
o: 1 micrometer
1 centimeter
1 dekameter
1 kilometer
1 decimeter
S.w: 1 km = 1,000 m; 1 dam = 10 m; 1 dm = 0.1 m; 1 cm = 0.01 m; 1 micrometer = 0.000001 m (10⁻⁶ m). Deka (10) and deci (0.1) sound alike but sit on opposite sides of the base unit: King Henry Died By Drinking Chocolate Milk (kilo, hecto, deka, base, deci, centi, milli), with micro three steps below milli.

S.q: In a water molecule, the oxygen atom pulls the shared electrons more strongly than the hydrogen atoms do. Which choice correctly describes the O-H bonds and the water molecule as a whole?
o: Polar covalent bonds in a linear, nonpolar molecule
Polar covalent bonds in a bent, polar molecule
Ionic bonds in a bent molecule with full charges
Nonpolar covalent bonds in a bent, polar molecule
S.w: Unequal sharing makes each O-H bond polar covalent: oxygen gets a partial negative charge and each hydrogen a partial positive charge. Because the molecule is bent, the bond polarities do not cancel, so water is a polar molecule.

n.0: Water is bent, not linear. A linear shape (as in CO₂) would let the bond polarities cancel.
n.2: Electrons are shared, not fully transferred, between oxygen and hydrogen, so there are partial charges, not full ionic charges.
n.3: Nonpolar bonds involve equal sharing; oxygen's stronger pull makes the O-H bonds polar.

S.q: Analysis of a sample of double-stranded DNA shows that 22% of its bases are thymine. What percentage of its bases are guanine? Enter your answer as a whole-number percent.

tr.22: assumed guanine equals thymine instead of adenine
tr.56: found G + C but did not split it between G and C
tr.78: subtracted thymine once from 100 and stopped

S.w: Step 1: A = T, so A is also 22%, and A + T = 44%. Step 2: G + C = 100% - 44% = 56%. Step 3: G = C, so G = 56% / 2 = 28%.

S.q: Researchers isolate a new bacterium from every sick animal in an outbreak and grow it in pure culture. According to Koch's postulates, what should they do next?
o: Treat the sick animals with an antibiotic and record recovery.
Re-isolate the bacterium from a newly infected animal.
Find the bacterium in each diseased animal in the outbreak.
Introduce the cultured bacterium into a healthy animal.
S.w: Koch's postulates: (1) the microbe is found in all diseased hosts, (2) it is isolated and grown in pure culture, (3) it causes the disease when introduced into a healthy host, (4) it is re-isolated from that host. Steps 1 and 2 are done, so step 3 is next.

n.0: Treating with antibiotics is not one of Koch's postulates and would not show that the microbe causes the disease.
n.1: Re-isolating the microbe is the final step (4); it can only follow infection of a healthy host.
n.2: Finding the microbe in all diseased hosts is step 1, which the researchers have already done.
